_note: Round 55: the topic and group pages (pipeline/seo_topics.mjs, written with the other static pages by seo_pages.mjs). One entry = one page; every figure comes from the map at deploy. Fields: slug; kind 'topic' (/<slug>/) or 'group' (/group/<slug>/); label (the link text in the home page's Topics list); title (at most 60 characters) and description (at most 155), each a string or a list of forms, the first that fits is used; h1; intro; rank: the measure the table is ranked by (net, ua, rus, frozen, paid, paidGain, aid, kiel, or part:<key> for one part of the panel); order: desc (high to low; for net and rus that is from the Ukraine side) or asc (from the Russia side); sort: gdp (% of GDP), eur or pp (per person); columns: the other measures shown; members: ISO codes of a group, or regions: the map's regions (eu, eur, am, asia, mea); exclude: ISO codes left out; minGdp: smallest economy ranked (€ bn, default 5 for gdp and pp, 0 for eur); nonzero: leave out countries whose ranked measure is zero; limit: rows shown; map: the map's address to open (#view=rank&lens=support ...); faq: questions, each answered with {placeholders} filled from the table (see seo_topics.mjs); sections: extra paragraphs or lists; notes: short lines under the table; subtotals: group slugs whose totals are shown too; related: slugs of related pages. Placeholders in title, description, intro, faq, sections and notes: {n} (rows in the table) {members} (a group's members) {dataTo} {top1} {top2} {top3} {top3list} {top1_eur} {top1_pct} {top1_pp}; {sum:KEY_eur} {sum:KEY_pct} {sum:KEY_pp} (members' best estimates added, % of their combined GDP); {nToU:KEY} {nToR:KEY} {nUnsure:KEY} (counts by the panel's chance level) and {namesToU:KEY} {namesToR:KEY} {namesUnsure:KEY} (their names); {top1by:KEY} {top3by:KEY} {top1by:KEY_eur} (the largest by another measure); {sub:SLUG:KEY_eur} {sub:SLUG:KEY_pct} {sub:SLUG:n} (a subtotal and its count); {iso:ISO:KEY_eur} and {iso:ISO:KEY_pct} (one named country's figure); {name:ISO} and {the:ISO} (a country's name, the map's: 'United States', 'the United States'); {memberNames} {partyList}; {word:KEY} and {wordCap:KEY} (the map's own chance words: sure, lean, unc, near, zero, party). Round 57 (owner: wording that cannot go stale): words that depend on the data are written as conditions, {if:COND|words if true|words if false}, where COND compares values such as sum:paid, sum:ua, sub:eu:ua, iso:USA:ua, top1:rus, n, members, nParty, nToR:net (> < >= <= == != and ~ for within 2%; abs(sum:paid) for a size), e.g. '{sum:paid_eur}, {if:abs(sum:paid)~abs(sum:ua)|about the same as|{if:abs(sum:paid)>abs(sum:ua)|more than|less than}} the {sum:ua_eur}'; {q:words} marks a neutral question or topic name. Every text field is read by the wording guard (seo_check.py, check 48): no number, ranking (most, largest, first ...), comparison, direction (toward Ukraine or Russia, helps, supports), certainty (likely, very likely, too close to call ...), trend or absolute word outside a placeholder or condition; a sentence that is a question may ask about direction, ranking or comparison. Round 56: rank may also be armed (weapons and troops sent to Russia at full value); order abs ranks by size either way; side 'cost' marks a measure outside the totals; moneyNote 'mil' says how weapons sent to Russia count.

pages.h1: Ukraine support tracker: aid, refugees and trade with Russia, every country
pages.intro: Support for Ukraine from February 2022 to {dataTo} for every country, sorted by euros: its own aid (loans at their gift value), its share of EU aid and the cost of hosting refugees, minus money flowing back, each also as a share of GDP and per person. Beside it, the net: support plus how much less, or more, Russia kept from trade with that country than in a world without the war. In euros, the table starts with {top3list}.

faq.q: Which countries give the most to Ukraine?
faq.a: In euros since 2022 the table starts with {top3list}: {top1} {top1_eur}. Together the {n} countries in this table gave {sum:ua_eur}. As a share of GDP the order changes; each row gives both, and per person.

faq.q: How is this different from an aid-only tracker?
faq.a: It adds what aid-only trackers do not measure: the change in what Russia kept from each country's trade against a world without the war, the return Russia lost on money frozen there, refugee hosting, loans at their gift value and money flowing back to the donor. With all of that, {nToU:net} of the countries listed are {word:sure} toward Ukraine and {nToR:net} {word:sure} toward Russia.

faq.q: Where do the aid figures come from?
faq.a: Government aid starts from the Kiel Institute's Ukraine Support Tracker, adjusted: donated weapons at their market value, loans at their gift value, military aid counted when delivered. The Kiel column shows the Institute's own published figure for each country's aid next to what is counted here. Refugee hosting, EU shares and money flowing back come from other official sources, listed on each country page.

sections.h2: What we count that aid-only trackers don't
list: Trade with Russia against a no-war baseline: how much more or less Russia kept from each country's trade (taxes and profit above a normal return, not the sales value) than in a world without the war.
Frozen Russian money: the return Russia lost on its reserves and private assets frozen in each country, in the net, not in support or trade.
Refugee hosting: what each country spent hosting people who fled Ukraine.
Loans at their gift value: a loan counts for the part that is a gift (its grant element), not its full amount.
Money flowing back: aid spent in the donor's own economy and extra sales to Ukraine are subtracted at the seller's real gain.

p: War Balance is not affiliated with the Kiel Institute's Ukraine Support Tracker; we use its aid data as one of our sources.

The Kiel column is the Institute's published figure for each country's own aid (military, financial and humanitarian). It differs from the aid counted here where weapons are valued at market value, loans count at their gift value, military aid counts when delivered and G7 loans repaid from Russian assets are left out. A dash means the Institute does not list the country.

pages.h1: Who bought Russian oil and gas? What each country paid Russia since 2022
pages.intro: This page lists what each country paid Russia from February 2022 to {dataTo}, sorted by euros and starting with {top3list} ({top1}: {top1_eur}), and shows how much more or less Russia kept from those purchases than in a world without the war, the extra it earned from war-time fuel prices and the Russian oil bought refined in other countries.

faq.q: Who buys Russian oil and gas?
faq.a: By what they paid Russia from 2022 to {dataTo}, the table starts with {top3list}: {top1} paid {top1_eur}. The {n} countries listed paid {sum:paid_eur} in all. The model does not split these payments by fuel for the war years; the fuel share column gives the share of fuel in each country's purchases before the war (2018 to 2021).

faq.q: Did buying Russian fuel help Russia?
faq.a: What counts is not the sales value but how much more or less Russia kept (taxes and profit) than without the war. From the purchases of the {n} countries listed, Russia kept {sum:paidGain_eur} {if:sum:paidGain>=0|less|more} than in a world without the war, with what each of them would then have bought. War-time fuel prices and Russian oil refined elsewhere are shown separately.

faq.q: How much Russian oil did each country buy, in barrels?
faq.a: This site does not give volumes. It measures money: what was paid to Russia, and the change in what Russia kept from it. For volumes, see energy trade trackers and customs statistics.

sections.h2: What the data can and cannot say
p: The model does not separate oil, gas and other goods in what each country paid Russia during the war: "Paid Russia" is everything bought from Russia, recorded in customs and partner data (fuel and other goods, services, company taxes in Russia, gold and other payments). The fuel share column is from before the war (2018 to 2021) and shows how much of a country's purchases from Russia were fuel then.
The parts about fuel: the extra Russia earned from war-time fuel prices, and Russian oil bought after refining in another country. Volumes (barrels, cubic metres) are not given here.

notes: Paid Russia: recorded payments since 2022, gross. The fuel columns are parts of what Russia kept from its purchases.

pages.h1: Frozen Russian assets: what Russia lost on money frozen in each country
pages.intro: Russia's central bank reserves and Russian private assets frozen abroad since 2022 earn Russia nothing. The number here is the return Russia lost on them from February 2022 to {dataTo}, not the amount frozen: {sum:frozen_eur} across the {n} countries listed; in {top1} it comes to {top1_eur}.

faq.q: Where are frozen Russian assets held?
faq.a: By the return Russia lost on them since 2022, the table starts with {top3list}. In {top1} the lost return comes to {top1_eur} ({top1_pct} of one year's GDP).

faq.q: Is the frozen money counted as aid to Ukraine?
faq.a: No. The return Russia lost on frozen money is its own line, added to the net: it is not support for Ukraine and not part of what Russia kept from trade. Loans to Ukraine repaid from the proceeds of Russian assets are left out of donors' aid, since Russia pays for them.

faq.q: Why not show the amount frozen?
faq.a: The scale of the site is money moved toward Ukraine or Russia over the war. A frozen amount is a stock that still belongs to Russia; what Russia loses each year is the return it would have earned, so that is what is counted.

notes: The return Russia lost, since 2022: reserves (central bank) and private Russian assets, each with its range.

faq.a: Yes, as earnings from trade with Russia: the extra income a country's firms made carrying and insuring Russian oil counts in its trade with Russia, like a sale to Russia, at the firms' net gain. The oil sale itself counts under the buyer's trade.

faq.q: Has Europe given more to Ukraine than the US?
faq.a: EU members together gave {sub:eu:ua_eur} since 2022 ({sub:eu:ua_pct} of their combined GDP), {the:USA} {iso:USA:ua_eur} ({iso:USA:ua_pct} of its GDP). Both figures count aid with loans at their gift value and refugee hosting; the Kiel column gives the Institute's own figure for each country's aid.

pages.h1: Who sends Russia weapons? Military supplies to Russia since 2022
pages.intro: Weapons, ammunition and troops sent to Russia from February 2022 to {dataTo}, by sending country, at their full value as Russia's panel lists them, beside what counts in the totals: what Russia paid for counts at the seller's net gain, like a sale; what it did not pay for counts in full. The evidence is thinner than for trade, so the figures are rough.{if:nParty| {partyList}, parties to the war, are listed apart.|} Dual-use goods in recorded trade count under trade.

faq.q: Is {name:IRN} sending drones to Russia?
faq.a: Yes. {name:IRN}'s Shahed drones and missiles delivered under contract since 2022 come to about {iso:IRN:armed_eur} at full value, from the sources on its page.

faq.q: Are {name:PRK}'s troops counted?
faq.a: Yes: {name:PRK}'s shells, missiles and troops come to about {iso:PRK:armed_eur} at full value since 2022. As a party to the war (with Russia) it is listed apart and not ranked.

faq.q: Is {name:CHN} sending weapons to Russia?
faq.a: What is counted here is what is not in recorded trade (unrecorded military items, smuggled dual-use goods, services): about {iso:CHN:armed_eur} at full value since 2022, a rough estimate. Recorded dual-use exports already count under {name:CHN}'s trade with Russia.

pages.h1: Russian oil price cap: who bought Russian crude at a discount?
pages.intro: Since March 2022 Russia has sold crude below Brent, under the EU embargo and the G7 price cap. This page sorts the discount each buyer gained from then to {dataTo}, counting the part beyond Russia's normal pre-war discount: for {top1} it comes to {top1_eur}. It is shown for information and not added to the totals: what Russia kept from each buyer, discounts included, is in its trade figures.

faq.q: How big is the discount on Russian oil?
faq.a: Across the {n} buyers listed, the discount gained since March 2022 beyond Russia's normal pre-war discount comes to {sum:part:disc_eur}; the table starts with {top3list}.

faq.q: Did the price cap reduce Russia's oil income?
faq.a: Partly. Selling at a discount cut what Russia kept, but war-time prices raised it, in 2022 in particular; each buyer's page shows both in its line for war-time fuel prices.

pages.h1: Trade hubs and Russia: what passes through the UAE, Türkiye and Central Asia
pages.intro: From February 2022 to {dataTo}, Russia kept {sum:rus_eur} {if:sum:rus>=0|less|more} from trade with these {members} hubs together than without the war. Goods they passed on to Russia count for the countries that made them; each hub keeps its trading margin here.

faq.q: Is Kazakhstan helping Russia evade sanctions?
faq.a: Goods made elsewhere and sold on to Russia through {name:KAZ} count here for the countries that made them, so {name:KAZ}'s own figure covers its own trade and its trading margin.{if:nToR:net| {wordCap:sure} toward Russia among these hubs: {namesToR:net}.|}

faq.q: Why are re-exports not counted for the hub?
faq.a: The money for re-exported goods goes mostly to the maker; the hub keeps a margin. Counting the maker shows whose goods reach Russia.

pages.h1: Russian oil through the back door: who bought fuel refined from Russian crude?
pages.intro: Diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in {name:IND}, {name:TUR}, {name:CHN}, {the:ARE} or EU refineries reach buyers elsewhere. For each buying country this page counts what Russia kept on the crude inside that fuel, against the pre-war level, from February 2022 to {dataTo}. The table starts with {top1} ({top1_eur} {if:top1:part:laund<0|more|less} for Russia); where buyers took less of it than before the war, Russia kept less.

faq.q: Does Europe still buy Russian oil through India?
faq.a: Some, as fuel refined from Russian crude in {name:IND}, {name:TUR} and elsewhere, until the EU's ban of 21 January 2026 on fuel made from Russian crude. Here such fuel counts for the buyer at what Russia kept on the crude inside it, against the pre-war level; each European country's page gives its own line.

faq.q: Is this legal?
faq.a: Mostly, until the EU's 2026 ban. The page measures money, not legality.
